findings.title: Row-lock concurrency guarantee asserted but verified nowhere
findings.why_it_matters: This batch's headline concurrency fix is `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the record row in `submit_approval` and `approval_step`, and the in-code comments state it as a hard guarantee: two concurrent submits must be "一胜一拒" and two concurrent approvals must produce exactly one `APPROVAL_STEP_PASSED` audit row. Nothing in the repository verifies that. The unit suite runs on in-memory SQLite, where SQLAlchemy's SQLite dialect compiles `with_for_update()` to an empty string (no lock at all). The new test that is supposed to cover this (`test_second_submit_after_commit_is_409`) is serial by construction and its own docstring hands the PG verification to the "CI fresh-PG api-drift job" — but the only workflow in this repo (`.github/workflows/check-api-drift.yml`) runs `alembic upgrade head`, the OpenAPI export/drift check, `check_migration_idempotency.py`, one visual-renderer test file and the frontend typecheck; it never runs the backend API tests and never issues a concurrent request. actionable_findings.why_it_matters: This batch's headline concurrency fix is `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the record row in `submit_approval` and `approval_step`, and the in-code comments state it as a hard guarantee: two concurrent submits must be "一胜一拒" and two concurrent approvals must produce exactly one `APPROVAL_STEP_PASSED` audit row. Verified: projects.project_no carries a real unique constraint (uq_projects_project_no), and every other NOT NULL column is supplied and validated by ProjectCreate, so the only other reachable integrity failure today is an fk_projects_workspace_id violation if the workspace is deleted between the existence check and the INSERT (FORMAL workspaces have retention_days=None, so the window is narrow). When it does fire, the API tells the user their project number is taken and changing the number does not help.

residual_risks.title: The project matrix binding is read after the record row lock, without locking the binding itself
residual_risks.detail: submit_approval takes the record row lock first and then reads the project's RECORD matrix binding, but that read is not itself locked. A rebind that commits between the read and the snapshot write leaves the snapshot holding the pre-rebind chain while the project already points at the new matrix. This is consistent with the intended freeze-at-submit semantics, but the frozen chain of a record submitted at time T depends on a read that is not atomic with the binding change.

residual_risks.title: submit_approval writes the snapshot before the transition that can reject it, leaving a mutated record in the session
residual_risks.detail: record.approval_chain_snapshot is written before the _transition call that can reject the submit with 409, so a rejected request leaves a mutated record in the session. This is safe today only because the production dependency get_db rolls back on exception and the test override closes (and therefore rolls back) the session when the endpoint raises; a future change that commits or reuses the session after a caught PcsError would persist the rejected submitter's snapshot.

triage_groups.title: Approval-chain snapshot: the row lock and the legacy-row fallback
triage_groups.context: The frozen snapshot mechanism claims two runtime guarantees: the submit path serializes concurrent submits with a FOR UPDATE row lock, and every approval step re-asserts the submitter (403 APPROVAL_SELF_REVIEW_FORBIDDEN). Neither guarantee is currently observed by an automated test, and the second one does not fire at all for rows that have no snapshot.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Handle #1 first: pin the lock at the SQL level (compile the locking SELECT against the PostgreSQL dialect and assert FOR UPDATE) and correct the false delegation to a CI job that does not run the backend suite. Then decide the policy for rows without a snapshot - derive the submitter from the RECORD_TRANSITION/SUBMIT_FOR_CHECK audit row, or make a NULL snapshot a loud 409 instead of a silent downgrade to the live matrix - and apply the chosen fix for #9.
triage_groups.why: Both live in the same approval path of records_actions.py and both decide whether the snapshot is trustworthy. A fixer stops at #9 because the legacy-row policy is a design choice; the mechanical half of #1 can be applied first without waiting.

triage_groups.title: p9_013 / p9_014 migration tests: guards and stale statements
triage_groups.context: The batch added two real-PostgreSQL engine-level tests and a 20-table migration, but the file still claims the verification is carried by a CI job that runs no pytest, the 20-table list has no guard against ORM drift, two docstrings describe the file's behaviour inaccurately, and the schema-cleanup failure is swallowed.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Fix #11 first (correct both docstrings to state that the api-drift job runs only alembic upgrade head and that the engine-level file must be run manually against a PostgreSQL instance; the PG-lane debt is already registered as TODO-099 and this repo has no CI/CD pipeline by standing decision). Then add the p9_014 test file for #5 (ORM leaf tables vs the migration's _TABLES, plus jsonb/nullability for all 20 tables), surface the cleanup return code for #18, and correct the two stale docstrings for #16 and #17.
triage_groups.why: All five sit in the same migration-test subsystem and can be done in one pass over tests/alembic/test_p9_013_bind_default_record_matrix.py plus the new p9_014 test file; #11's correction also removes the false claim that lets the rest read as covered.

triage_groups.title: Reference documentation for the new snapshot column
triage_groups.context: The compact ORM reference table still describes the 20 record tables without approval_chain_snapshot, and the batch's new solutions entry points at a wiki link to a document that does not exist.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Register the column in pcs-backend/docs/schema_compact_orm.md (#10) and repoint or create the linked note so the batch's third lesson has a real target (#15).
triage_groups.why: Both are documentation-registration obligations the batch already accepted once (the same commit updated the compact table for a dropped column), and both mislead exactly the readers the batch wanted to redirect - people hand-writing SQL or looking up how PG-only semantics are verified.

triage_groups.title: Deliverable page: contract-derived types and a runtime-safe label lookup
triage_groups.context: DeliverableProgressPage hand-copies the list envelope that the OpenAPI contract already defines, and its WORKFLOW_LABELS lookup lost its runtime fallback after workflow_type was narrowed to a three-value union against a contract whose schema is a bare string.

demoted_from_primary.title: No backfill: in-flight records keep the unbinding hole open
demoted_from_primary.why_it_matters: The batch's core fix is to freeze the approval chain at submit time. Records that were already `IN_APPROVAL` when this deploys have `approval_chain_snapshot IS NULL` — the migration only adds a nullable column and back-fills nothing — and for those rows the protection never switches on: `_next_approval_role` falls back to the live matrix (so a mid-flight rebind still rewrites the chain, which is exactly the self-approval path the batch set out to close), and the per-step self-review assertion at line 549 is skipped entirely because it is guarded on the snapshot being present. The window is therefore not "the deployment moment" but "until those specific records finish their chain", and nothing in the code, the migration, or the tests records that. This branch is also the one place with no test at all: every approval test in the tree goes through `submit-approval` first, so the snapshot-less path is never exercised. The practical exposure today is small only because the system is pre-production with few rows in flight; that is exactly the kind of assumption that quietly becomes a live hole the first time the app has real users.
